Tuesday: Joseph saved the swing next to his for Reena, like always. She came late, breathless, talking about her new dance class and a girl called Mitali. She stayed five minutes, then ran to the steps where Mitali was waiting.
Friday: Reena didn't come to the swings at all. Joseph kicked the gravel and went over everything. Was it because he'd laughed when she fell in the relay race? Because his tiffin smelled of fish? He couldn't find the thing he did.
The next Wednesday: At home, he told his mother, "Reena doesn't like me any more."
Amma asked, "Did she say that?"
He thought about it. She hadn't. She'd just been busy, rushing off to dance practice twice a week with Mitali. Somehow that felt a little better, and still a bit sad.

qa.q: What did Joseph save for Reena on Tuesday?
qa.a: Joseph saved the swing next to his for Reena.

qa.q: What was Joseph worried about as he went over everything on Friday?
qa.a: Joseph worried he had done something wrong to make Reena leave, like laughing when she fell in the relay or his tiffin smelling of fish. 😔

qa.q: What helped Joseph at this stage, and what else could he try?
qa.a: Amma's question helped Joseph see that Reena never said she disliked him; next he could ask Reena to the swings on a day without dance practice.

qa.a: Reena is probably excited and busy with her dance class and Mitali, and may not notice that Joseph is still waiting at the swings.

grounding: Shows a boy left behind by a drifting friend, wondering what he did, when the real cause is her new dance class and new company.

Your Dadu will tell you something, beta. When I was eleven, in Nashik, my best friend was Madhav. Every evening in January we flew kites from his terrace, shouting till our mothers called us down.
Then Madhav joined an evening tuition, and after that the colony cricket team. First he came up to the terrace every day, then twice a week, then not at all. Nobody fought. Nobody said anything.
I was sure I must have done something. I remembered the time I tore his best kite and wondered if he'd been angry all along. Every evening at five I felt a heavy, dull feeling in my stomach.
Years later, at a wedding, I asked him. He blinked. "Darshan? You? I was just so tired from tuition, yaar. I thought you'd found new friends."
So when your friend stops calling, don't decide too quickly that it's you.

qa.q: Where did Darshan and Madhav fly kites every evening in January?
qa.a: They flew kites from Madhav's terrace every evening in January.

qa.q: Why did Darshan feel heavy every evening at five?
qa.a: Darshan missed Madhav and was sure he had done something wrong, even wondering if the torn kite had made Madhav angry all along.

qa.q: What turning point does Darshan want the grandchild to take from this?
qa.a: Not to decide too quickly that a fading friend is rejecting you; asking gently, or waiting before blaming yourself, can show the real reason.

qa.q: How did Madhav see the same months?
qa.a: Madhav was just tired from tuition and busy with cricket, and even thought Darshan had found new friends, so there was no rejection on his side.

grounding: Illustrates a boy left behind by a fading friendship who assumes he did something wrong, when the real cause was his friend's busier days.

Gurleen hung back by the colony gate while the other kids played. Across the park, Nilesh was laughing with his new cycling gang. Last year the two of them had built a whole mud city behind Block C.
"He doesn't even look at me now," she said.
Papa crouched beside her. "Maybe he's just busy. Want to go and say hello? Only hello."
She walked over, heart thumping, and said, "Hi, Nilesh." He looked surprised, then smiled. "Hi!"
That evening, with Papa's help, she sent a message to Nilesh's mother: "Can Nilesh come for one game of carrom on Sunday?" He came. It wasn't like the mud-city days; they talked about different things now.
At bedtime Papa said, "Some friends are for one season, some for many. The mud city was still real." Gurleen thought about that for a long time.

qa.q: What had Gurleen and Nilesh built together last year?
qa.a: They had built a whole mud city behind Block C.

qa.q: How was Gurleen feeling as she walked across the park?
qa.a: Gurleen was nervous, with her heart thumping, but also hoping Nilesh would still say hello. 😰

qa.q: Which steps did Papa use to help Gurleen, and why did they work?
qa.a: Papa suggested only a hello, then helped invite Nilesh for one carrom game, and explained that friends can change by season; small steps kept it kind without pressure.

qa.q: How might Nilesh feel when Gurleen says hello?
qa.a: Nilesh seemed surprised and then pleased, so he probably hadn't meant to leave Gurleen out; he was just busy with his new cycling gang.

grounding: Shows a parent helping a child greet an old friend, invite him to one game, and accept that friendships can belong to different seasons without being false.

passage:
I'm Chinmay, and in my first month at the hostel in Manipal I said yes to everything. Instant noodles on the terrace at midnight, yes. A trip to the beach at six in the morning, yes. A quiz club I had no interest in, also yes. My room felt too quiet otherwise.
Thomas was in the room opposite, from Kottayam. On the fourth night we both admitted we'd cried after our parents left. By the second week we were sharing a toothpaste tube and finishing each other's jokes, and I told Amma on the phone that I'd found my best friend.
Looking back, I'm a little embarrassed by how fast I said that. We'd known each other eleven days. The warmth was real, but a lot of it was two homesick boys holding on to the first person who understood. We're still friends. Just the ordinary, slower kind.

qa.q: What did Thomas and Chinmay admit on the fourth night?
qa.a: They both admitted they'd cried after their parents left.

qa.q: Why did Chinmay say yes to every invitation in the first month?
qa.a: Chinmay was lonely and the room felt too quiet otherwise, so every plan was a way not to be alone.

qa.q: What could Chinmay keep in mind during this open-door stage?
qa.a: Chinmay could enjoy the quick warmth while letting friendships grow at their own pace, instead of naming someone a best friend after eleven days.

qa.q: How might Thomas have felt in those first weeks?
qa.a: Thomas was homesick too, so finding Chinmay across the corridor probably felt like relief and a safe person to hold on to.

grounding: Shows a lonely, eager first-year hostel student saying yes to everything and forming a quick, homesick closeness that felt stronger than it yet was.

Saurabh (from Patna, first job, first time living away from home) has joined every plan in the batch so far: the Friday biryani run, the Sunday fort trek, even the badminton group, though he told me he "can't really play". He is always the first to reply "I'm in" on the batch group.

The power went out at eleven, the night before the accounts exam, and the hostel generator coughed and died. Ankita and Jyoti gave up revising by phone torch and lay on their beds in the dark.
"Can I tell you something?" Ankita said. "My parents barely speak now. Papa sleeps at the shop some nights." She waited, heart loud, for Jyoti to change the subject.
Jyoti didn't. "That sounds so lonely for you," she said. After a pause: "I'm scared I'll fail this course and my mother will say she knew it." Then, quieter: "And I still check my ex's profile. Two years later. Pathetic."
"Not pathetic," Ankita said. "I did the same with mine for a whole summer."
When the lights came back at one, neither of them reached for their notes straight away. They'd have to cram at dawn, but it felt as if they'd both passed a test they hadn't studied for.

qa.q: When did the lights come back?
qa.a: The lights came back at one.

qa.q: Why did Ankita wait with her heart loud after speaking?
qa.a: Ankita was afraid Jyoti might change the subject; she was checking whether Jyoti would respond with care.

qa.q: What made this conversation deepen the friendship?
qa.a: Each disclosure was met with care and matched: Jyoti named Ankita's loneliness and shared her own fears, and Ankita answered 'Not pathetic' with a story of her own. 🤍

qa.q: What would change if Jyoti had changed the subject?
qa.a: Ankita would likely feel exposed and pull back, and the friendship might have stayed on the surface instead of becoming real.

grounding: Shows two hostel friends trading family troubles, career fears and old heartbreak, each watching whether the other responds with care.

The bakery near the college gate in Hyderabad was nearly empty at four. Rehana stirred her tea for too long before she said it: her engagement had been called off in the summer, and her khala still brought it up at every family dinner.
Jyoti put down her puff. She'd known Rehana for five months, mostly as a lab partner. For a second she didn't know what to say, then chose honesty. "I didn't know. I'm sorry. That must feel like it's on display all the time."
Rehana nodded, eyes on the cup.
Jyoti took a breath. "Can I tell you mine? I'm terrified I won't get placed. Papa's shop closed in March and everyone's counting on me."
Rehana looked up properly then. "You carry that into lab every day, alone?"
They stayed till the owner started stacking chairs. On the walk to the bus stop, Jyoti kept thinking: she told me first, and she didn't flinch at mine.

qa.a: Rehana said her engagement had been called off in the summer.

qa.a: Jyoti felt trusted and safe: Rehana had told her first and didn't flinch at her fears, so the friendship now felt real.

I'm Francis, and I share a lab bench with Samir, so I see his group every day. There are five of them. They eat lunch at the same corner table in the canteen, near the water cooler, and nobody else sits there. Nobody was told not to; it's just understood. They study in the back room of the library, split cab fares home at Diwali, and have a group name I've never heard said aloud.
They look comfortable. Nobody has to plan who to sit with. Nobody eats alone.
But last month the debate club put up a poster, and Samir stood in front of it for a long time. When I asked if he'd join, he laughed and said, "The guys would think I've gone posh." He didn't sign up. Maybe he didn't want to. I can't tell. But he looked back at the poster twice on the way out.

qa.q: Where does Samir's group eat lunch?
qa.a: They eat lunch at the same corner table in the canteen, near the water cooler.

qa.q: What might Samir have been feeling in front of the debate poster?
qa.a: Samir may have wanted to join but worried the group would judge him; looking back twice suggests he was torn, though Francis can't be sure.

qa.a: Samir could try the debate club anyway and mention it lightly to the group; a secure friendship can stretch to make room for other interests.

qa.a: To Francis the group looks comfortable and closed at once: nobody eats alone, yet nobody else sits at that table.

I'm Jasleen. After final year, our trio split three ways. I got a placement in Bengaluru. Rajni met a guy from her office in Delhi and suddenly had plans every weekend. Noor stayed back home and took tuition batches to help pay her brother's fees, so she was always tired.
At first we did Sunday video calls. Then every other Sunday. Then someone would cancel, usually me, because of a deadline. Now I mostly know Rajni's life through her posts. I like them. She likes mine.
Last month I saw her birthday photos and realised I hadn't called. I felt sick with guilt.
Then Rajni messaged: "Sorry I've gone missing, I keep meaning to call you." She felt it too. Neither of us had stopped caring. We just both kept waiting to be the one with free time.

Counselling note. Student: Rukmini, final year B.Com. Session 2.
Rukmini came in about placement stress, but most of the session was about her friends. Her group of three was very close through college. Now Aparna is in a relationship and busy most evenings, Deepa is working part-time because money is tight at home, and Rukmini has an offer in Chennai starting in July.
She showed me her phone: a string of hearts and "miss u" replies on Aparna's photos, and no real conversation in six weeks. "I keep thinking I should call. Then I think, she's the busy one, why should I always call?" Then, softer: "Maybe she's thinking the same about me."
She seemed relieved to say it aloud. We talked about how friends taking different paths is normal and not a verdict on the friendship. She plans to send Aparna a voice note tonight instead of another like. Will follow up next week.

Mentor meeting note, Tuesday. Divyansh, third year.
Divyansh was quiet today. When I asked about his week, he said he'd been scrolling back through his chat with Mohit, his school friend from Indore, and realised their last proper conversation was in February. It is September now. "We didn't fight or anything," he said. "Nothing happened. That's what's weird. I can't even be angry at anyone."
He said he feels silly being sad about "basically nothing" when other people have real problems. He kept clicking his pen cap on and off.
I told him that a friendship slowly going quiet is still a loss, and it is all right to feel sad about it without a big reason. He looked surprised at that, then a little relieved.
I suggested he could write to Mohit if he wanted, or simply let himself miss him for now. Will check in next week.

qa.q: When was Divyansh's last proper conversation with Mohit?
qa.a: Their last proper conversation was in February.

qa.q: Why does Divyansh feel silly for being sad?
qa.a: Divyansh thinks the sadness has no real cause, since nothing happened and there was no fight, so it feels like being sad about 'basically nothing'.

qa.q: How did the mentor help Divyansh at this stage?
qa.a: The mentor named the fading as a real loss, gave Divyansh permission to feel sad, and offered choices: write to Mohit or simply miss him for now.

qa.q: How might Mohit be experiencing these same months?
qa.a: Mohit may not have noticed the gap at all, or may feel the same quiet sadness without saying it, since there was never any fight.

grounding: Shows a young man realising months have passed since a real talk with his school friend and feeling sad with nothing to blame, and a mentor allowing that grief.

Sunday night
Santosh posted a photo today from a trek. With people I don't know. And it hit me: I didn't know he'd gone. I didn't even know he liked trekking now.
I scrolled up our chat. Last real message: 12 May, about my cousin's wedding. After that, just birthday wishes and one forwarded joke. Four months.
We didn't fight. Nobody left. There's nothing I can point to and say, that's when. That makes it worse somehow, because who do I tell? "My friend is fine and we just stopped talking"? Sounds like nothing.
But it doesn't feel like nothing. It feels like when Nani's house was sold. Same rooms, just not ours any more.
Maybe I'm allowed to be sad about this. I think I am.
Lalit

qa.a: The last real message was about Lalit's cousin's wedding, on 12 May.

qa.q: Why does the lack of a fight make Lalit feel worse?
qa.a: With nothing to point to, Lalit feels no one would accept it as a reason to be sad, so the hurt has nowhere to go.

qa.q: What could Lalit do next with this sadness?
qa.a: Lalit could let the grief be real, talk about it with someone close, and decide whether to message Santosh about the trek to see what is still worth keeping.

qa.q: How might Santosh see the last four months?
qa.a: Santosh has probably just been busy with new people and trekking and may not see the silence as an ending at all.

grounding: Illustrates quiet grief when a friendship fades with no single event to blame, a loss that feels hard to mourn openly.

passage:
On a grey Saturday in Melbourne, Tuan found an old photo on his phone: him and Tomas on the fire escape of their student flat, eating pho from the place downstairs, both squinting into the sun. Tomas had moved to Adelaide for work a year ago. They'd traded likes since, not much else.
Tuan typed "Hey, how's things?" and deleted it. Too easy to answer with "good, you?"
Instead he wrote: "Found a photo of us on the fire escape with pho. I miss those Fridays. Free for a call Sunday evening?"
Tomas replied within ten minutes. "Mate. Yes. I still can't find decent pho here."
Later, scrolling, Tuan passed the group chat from his old five-a-side team, silent for months. He thought about reviving it, then just sent, "Great seasons, all of you. Thanks for them," and muted it without guilt.

qa.q: Where had Tomas moved for work?
qa.a: Tomas had moved to Adelaide for work a year ago.

qa.q: Why did Tuan delete 'Hey, how's things?'
qa.a: Tuan felt it was too easy to answer with 'good, you?' and wanted a message that would actually reopen the friendship.

qa.q: Why did Tuan's second message work better?
qa.a: It named a specific shared memory and asked for a specific call time, making it easy for Tomas to say yes.

qa.q: How might the old teammates feel reading Tuan's thanks?
qa.a: They would likely feel appreciated rather than dropped, since Tuan closed that chapter warmly instead of letting it fade in silence.

grounding: Shows a young man reaching out with a specific memory and call time to a friend worth keeping, while letting another tie go with thanks.

In the reading room of the women's hostel, Sarika was meant to be revising pharmacology. Instead she was looking at two names on her phone.
The first was Irawati, who had sat next to her from Class 6 to 12 in Nagpur. They hadn't really talked since Irawati started law school in Pune. Sarika missed her laugh more than she'd admitted.
The second was Pallavi, from coaching classes, who had only ever messaged when she needed notes.
She typed to Irawati: "Remember Sunday poha at your Aaji's? I was thinking of it today. Call on Saturday?"
Then she opened Pallavi's chat, wrote, "All the best for your exams, and thanks for the coaching-days company," and let that be enough.
The warden walked past and tapped the desk. Sarika put the phone face down and turned a page. Ten minutes later Irawati's reply, a row of yellow hearts, lit up the screen.

qa.a: Sarika asked Irawati to call on Saturday.

qa.q: What does Sarika feel about Irawati, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Sarika misses Irawati, especially her laugh, more than she'd admitted, which is why she reaches out with a specific memory. 🙂

qa.q: What is wise about how Sarika handled the two friendships?
qa.a: Sarika put effort into the friendship that mattered and let the other one go kindly with thanks, instead of forcing both or dropping both.

qa.q: What would change if Sarika had only sent Irawati 'Hi'?
qa.a: Irawati might have replied politely and nothing more; the named memory and set day make a real conversation far more likely.

The local bus from Barhiya rattled over every pothole, and Ganga and Pushpa sat squeezed on the last seat, school bags on their knees.
"Can I tell you two things?" Ganga said, eyes on the window. "But you can't tell anyone. Not even your sister."
Pushpa hooked her little finger into Ganga's. "Tell."
"First, I think I like Farhan. From the science stall at the mela."
Pushpa's eyebrows shot up, but she only grinned.
"Second," Ganga said, quieter, "Baba hasn't been paid for the wheat yet. Maa sold her silver anklets last week. I'm scared I'll have to leave school after tenth."
Pushpa didn't say anything clever. She just squeezed Ganga's finger harder and said, "You won't carry that by yourself."
When the bus stopped at their village, Ganga jumped down first, and for the first time in days she was humming.

qa.a: Maa sold her silver anklets last week.

qa.q: How can you tell that telling Pushpa made Ganga feel lighter?
qa.a: Ganga jumped down first and was humming for the first time in days, which shows relief after sharing her worries. 😊

qa.q: What could Pushpa do to keep being a safe friend?
qa.a: Pushpa could keep both secrets, check in quietly about school and home, and help Ganga talk to a trusted adult such as a teacher if the fear about leaving school grows.

qa.q: What might it mean to Pushpa that Ganga trusted her?
qa.a: Pushpa likely feels honoured and responsible, holding something happy and something heavy for her friend.

grounding: Illustrates a teenage girl sharing a crush and her family's money worries with her closest friend as an act of trust, and feeling lighter afterwards.

Friday, 11 pm
Today at the canteen I sat with Arnab's group for the first time. They're the band kids, the ones everyone knows. They were talking about who likes whom, and Arnab turned to me: "You're friends with Moumita, na? Does she like anyone?"
And I said it. That she likes Ritwik from Section C. Everyone went "ooh" and Arnab laughed: "This girl knows all the gossip!" I felt... included. Like I'd paid an entry fee.
On the walk home I told myself it was nothing. Everyone has crushes. It's not like I told them about her dad's job.
But now it's night and I keep seeing Moumita's face when she told me, how she made me pinky-swear. Ritwik goes to Arnab's tuition. Of course he'll hear.
I feel sick. I wanted them to find me interesting, and I used her to do it.
Kalyani

qa.a: Kalyani could tell Moumita herself tomorrow, before Ritwik hears it from others, apologise without excuses and accept that Moumita may be angry.

qa.q: What might Moumita go through if the secret reaches Ritwik?
qa.a: Moumita could feel exposed and embarrassed, and deeply hurt that the pinky-swear meant so little.

grounding: Shows a teenage girl letting a friend's secret slip to seem interesting to a new group, calling it no big deal at first and feeling its weight later.
